fields.title: Ezekiel
fields.subtitle: Yechezkel, “God strengthens”
fields.description: The visions of a priest carried off to Babylon, who saw the glory of the LORD by a canal among the exiles: a storm out of the north, four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, and a throne above them all. Ezekiel eats a scroll as sweet as honey, is made a watchman for his people, acts out the siege of Jerusalem, and watches the glory leave the temple before the city falls. Then the message turns to hope: God himself will shepherd his scattered flock, give his people a new heart and put his Spirit within them, breathe life into a valley of dry bones, and return to a new temple from which a river flows to make everything live, in a city named “The LORD Is There.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Ezekiel?
qa.answer: The third of the major prophets in the Old Testament, the visions and messages of Ezekiel, a priest who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. Its forty-eight chapters fall into three parts: judgement on Jerusalem before its fall (chapters 1–24), oracles against the surrounding nations (25–32), and, after the news that the city has fallen (33:21), promises of restoration ending in the vision of a new temple (33–48). Its refrain, repeated more than sixty times, is “Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

qa.question: Who was Ezekiel, and when did he prophesy?
qa.answer: Ezekiel son of Buzi was a priest taken from Jerusalem to Babylon in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin, and settled among the exiles at Tel-abib by the Kebar Canal. He was called in 593 BC, the fifth year of the exile, and his last dated oracle comes from 571 BC. Unusually for a prophetic book, it is written almost entirely in the first person and carefully dated throughout. Most scholars, though not all, hold that the book substantially comes from Ezekiel himself, perhaps with some later arrangement by his disciples. He was a contemporary of Jeremiah, who was preaching in Jerusalem at the same time.

qa.question: What is the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37?
qa.answer: A vision in which God sets Ezekiel in a valley full of dry bones and asks, “Son of man, can these bones live?” At God’s command the prophet speaks to the bones, which come together and are covered with flesh, and then to the breath, which enters them so that they stand up “a huge army”. God explains that the bones are the people of Israel in exile, who say their hope is gone, and promises to open their graves, bring them home and put his Spirit in them. It is first a promise of national restoration, but Jews and Christians have long read it also as a pledge of the resurrection of the dead.

qa.question: What does Ezekiel mean by a new heart?
qa.answer: In Ezekiel 36:25–27 God promises to cleanse his people, take out their “heart of stone” and give them “a heart of flesh”, and put his own Spirit within them so that they follow his ways. It echoes Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant written on the heart, and adds the gift of the Spirit. Earlier, in 18:31, God commands the people to make themselves a new heart; Christian teachers have often explained the two together by saying that God commands what only he can give. Many readers hear the promise behind Jesus’s words about being “born of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5).

qa.question: How should Ezekiel’s temple vision and Gog and Magog be understood?
qa.answer: Christians read these chapters in different ways. Some take the battle with Gog (chapters 38–39) and the new temple (40–48) as forecasts of literal future events; others read them as visions that use the language of Ezekiel’s day to show God’s final victory over every enemy and his dwelling with his people for ever. The New Testament takes up both: Revelation names Gog and Magog in the last rebellion against God (20:8), and pictures the new Jerusalem with no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, and a river of the water of life with the tree of life on its banks, as in Ezekiel 47.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name, and Ezekiel’s frequent “Lord GOD” joins it to the word for “master”. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone out of your bodies and give you a heart of flesh.

— Ezekiel 36:26

Ezekiel is the strangest of the prophets, and one of the most hopeful. It opens with a storm out of the north, wheels within wheels, and the glory of God on a throne above the living creatures. It goes on to a prophet lying on his side for over a year, shaving his head with a sword, and eating a scroll that tastes like honey. It contains some of the hardest pages in the Bible. And it ends with dry bones rising to their feet, a river flowing out of the temple to make the Dead Sea fresh, and a city whose name is “The LORD Is There.”

Its prophet was a priest who, as far as we know, never served in the temple. Ezekiel son of Buzi was carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin and the leading families of Jerusalem, and lived among the exiles at Tel-abib, by the Kebar Canal. Five years later, in 593, the heavens opened. For more than twenty years he spoke to people who had lost their home and were about to lose their temple too, and his book asks what Jeremiah’s and Lamentations’ ask in their own ways: if God’s house is gone, is God gone too?

The shape of the book

Ezekiel is the most orderly of the prophetic books. It is told almost entirely in the first person, and more than a dozen of its sections are dated by the year of Jehoiachin’s exile, mostly in sequence, from the call in the fifth year (593 BC) to a last oracle in the twenty-seventh (571). The fall of Jerusalem divides it neatly in two:

  • Chapters 1–24: the call, and judgement on Jerusalem, spoken before the city fell.
  • Chapters 25–32: oracles against the nations around Judah, from Ammon to Tyre and Egypt.
  • Chapters 33–48: after the news of the fall, promises of restoration, ending in the great vision of the new temple and the land (40–48).

The hinge is a single sentence in 33:21. In the twelfth year of the exile a survivor arrives from Jerusalem and says, “The city has fallen!” Up to that point Ezekiel has been tearing down false hope. From that point he builds true hope.

Through the whole book runs one refrain, heard more than sixty times: “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” Everything God does in Ezekiel, in judgement and in mercy, is so that he will be known for who he is.

The vision by the canal (Ezekiel 1–3)

The book opens with an overwhelming vision. Out of a storm come four living creatures, each with four faces, a human face, a lion’s, an ox’s and an eagle’s; beside them are wheels whose rims are “full of eyes all around”, going wherever the Spirit goes; above them is a vault “glittering like ice”, and above that a throne, and on the throne “a figure that looked like a human being”, surrounded by fire and brightness. Ezekiel piles up “something like” and “what looked like” as language strains at its limits, and then says what he has seen:

Like a rainbow in the clouds on a day of rain, so was the brightness on every side. This was what the likeness of the glory of the LORD looked like. When I saw it, I fell face down, and I heard the voice of someone speaking.

— Ezekiel 1:28

The point of all the strangeness is where it happens. The glory of the LORD, which had filled the temple in Jerusalem, has appeared by a canal in Babylon, among exiles. The throne has wheels. God is not confined to his house, and he has not abandoned his people.

Then God speaks, and his first words set the tone of the whole book: “Son of man, stand up on your feet.” The title, used over ninety times, means “human being”, “mortal”, and it reminds the prophet of the distance between himself and the glory he has seen. He is sent to “a rebellious house”, told that they may not listen, and given a scroll written on both sides with “laments and mourning and woe”. He is told to eat it, and “in my mouth it tasted as sweet as honey.” Then the Spirit carries him off, and he sits among the exiles for seven days, stunned.

He is appointed a watchman (3:17). If he warns the wicked and they do not turn, they die for their sin; if he fails to warn them, God will hold him responsible. The image returns at the turning point of the book (33:1–9), and it has shaped how preachers have thought about their calling ever since.

A prophet as a sign (Ezekiel 4–24)

Ezekiel does not only speak his message; he acts it out. He builds a model of Jerusalem under siege and lies beside it on his left side, and then on his right, bearing the years of his people’s guilt. He eats rationed bread cooked over dung. He shaves his head and beard with a sword, burns a third of the hair, strikes a third with the sword and scatters a third to the wind, keeping only a few strands tucked into his robe. He digs through a wall at night with his baggage on his shoulder, like a refugee. For long periods he is struck silent, able to speak only when God gives him a word (3:26–27).

The hardest sign of all is in chapter 24. God tells him that “the delight of your eyes” will be taken from him at a stroke, and that he must not mourn: “in the morning I spoke to the people, and that evening my wife died.” His silent grief becomes a sign for the exiles of the grief that will be too great for mourning when the temple, the delight of their eyes, is destroyed. No prophet’s life was more completely given over to the message.

The glory leaves the temple (Ezekiel 8–11)

In chapter 8 the Spirit lifts Ezekiel by a lock of his hair and carries him in visions to Jerusalem. He is shown what is happening in the temple: an idol at the north gate, elders burning incense to images in a dark room, women weeping for the god Tammuz, men bowing to the sun with their backs to the sanctuary. God asks him whether he sees the things that “will drive me far from my sanctuary”.

And then the glory goes. Step by step it rises from the inner sanctuary to the threshold, from the threshold to the cherubim, out to the east gate, and finally “went up from the middle of the city and stopped over the mountain east of the city.” The holiest thing in Israel’s life has left of its own accord. The Babylonians will burn an empty house.

Yet in the same vision comes a word for the exiles whom the people in Jerusalem despised: “for a little while I have still been a sanctuary to them in the lands they have gone to.” God himself will be their temple in Babylon. And he promises what he will do for them there: “I will take the heart of stone out of their bodies and give them a heart of flesh.”

Unfaithful Jerusalem, and a just God (Ezekiel 16–23)

Some of Ezekiel’s parables are the most shocking pages in Scripture. Chapter 16 tells of a baby girl abandoned at birth, “thrashing about in your blood”, whom the LORD passes by and tells to live, raises, marries and adorns, and who turns to prostitution with every passer-by. Chapter 23 tells of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, in even more graphic language. Ancient Jewish teachers restricted the public reading of some of these passages, and readers today find them painful. Their purpose is to make the exiles feel what idolatry is: not a change of religious taste, but the betrayal of a love that saved them. And even chapter 16 ends with a promise: “I myself will remember the covenant I made with you in your youth.”

Chapter 18 answers a proverb the exiles were repeating: “The parents eat sour grapes, but it is the children whose teeth are set on edge.” They believed they were being punished for their ancestors’ sins and could do nothing about it. God replies that every life belongs to him, and each person answers for their own way. The wicked who turn will live; the righteous who turn to wickedness will not be saved by their past. And beneath the logic is a plea:

Throw away all the rebellious acts you have committed, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why would you die, house of Israel? The death of anyone gives me no pleasure, declares the Lord GOD. So turn back and live!

— Ezekiel 18:31–32

The command to make a new heart in chapter 18 and the promise to give one in chapter 36 sit side by side in the book. Christians have discussed ever since how the two belong together. Most have answered that God commands what only he can give, and gives what he commands.

The nations (Ezekiel 25–32)

While the siege goes on, Ezekiel turns to the neighbours who were gloating over Judah. The longest oracles are against Tyre, the rich trading city on the coast, pictured as a great ship that sinks with all its cargo (27), and against Egypt, the power Judah kept trusting for rescue. The lament over the king of Tyre in chapter 28 pictures him as a figure in Eden, “on God’s holy mountain”, perfect until wickedness was found in him and cast out for his pride. Some early Christian writers read the passage as a description of the fall of Satan behind the king; others read it as a portrait of a human ruler in the language of Eden. Either way the lesson is the same as the charge God lays against the prince of Tyre in 28:2: “You are a mortal and not a god.”

The good shepherd and the new heart (Ezekiel 33–36)

When the news of the fall arrives, Ezekiel’s silence ends, and his message turns. Chapter 34 condemns Israel’s rulers as shepherds who fed themselves and left the flock to be scattered: “You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bandaged the injured.” Then God says he will do it himself:

For the Lord GOD says this: I myself will search for my flock and look after them. I myself will take care of my flock and let them lie down in rest, declares the Lord GOD. I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bandage the injured and strengthen the sick, but the fat and strong ones I will destroy. I will tend the flock with justice.

— Ezekiel 34:11, 15–16

He will also set over them “one shepherd, my servant David”. Six centuries later, Jesus stood in Jerusalem and said, “I am the good shepherd.”

Chapter 36 is the heart of Ezekiel’s hope. God will act, he says, not for Israel’s sake but for the sake of his holy name, which they have dragged through the mud among the nations. He will gather them, and then:

I will sprinkle pure water over you, and you will be clean. From all your impurities and from all your idols I will make you clean. I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone out of your bodies and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you and make you follow my statutes and carefully keep my rulings.

— Ezekiel 36:25–27

It is the same promise Jeremiah heard, of a covenant written on the heart, with one addition that changes everything: “I will put my Spirit within you.” Many readers have heard it behind Jesus’s words to Nicodemus, that no one can enter God’s kingdom unless they are “born of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5).

The valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37)

The best-known vision in the book follows at once. The hand of the LORD sets Ezekiel down in a valley full of bones, “and they were very dry.” God asks him, “Son of man, can these bones live?” and he gives the only honest answer: “Lord GOD, only you know.” He is told to prophesy to the bones, and they come together with a rattling, bone to bone, and sinews and flesh and skin cover them; but there is no breath in them. Then he prophesies to the breath:

Then he told me, “Prophesy to the breath. Prophesy, son of man, and say to it, The Lord GOD says this: Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live.” So I prophesied as he had commanded me, and breath entered them. They came to life and stood up on their feet, a huge army.

— Ezekiel 37:9–10

In Hebrew one word, ruach, means breath, wind and spirit, and the chapter plays on all three. God explains the vision: the bones are the whole house of Israel, who say, “Our bones have dried up, our hope is gone; we are completely cut off.” He will open their graves and bring them home, and put his Spirit in them so that they live. The vision is first of all a promise of national rebirth after the death of exile. But it is told as a resurrection, and Jews and Christians alike have long read it as a pledge that God can and will raise the dead.

Gog, and the new temple (Ezekiel 38–48)

Chapters 38–39 tell of a last assault on restored Israel by Gog, of the land of Magog, at the head of a host from the ends of the earth, and of God’s decisive victory over him. Revelation takes up the names for the final rebellion against God (Revelation 20:8). Christians disagree about how to read these chapters, as a forecast of particular events at the end of history or as a picture, in the language of Ezekiel’s day, of the final defeat of every power that sets itself against God’s people. The chapters end on the promise, “I will pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel.”

The last nine chapters are a vision dated to the twenty-fifth year of the exile. An angelic guide with a measuring rod shows Ezekiel a new temple, wall by wall and gate by gate, with its altar, its priests and its offerings, and the land divided anew among the tribes. Then the glory that left by the east gate in chapter 11 comes back the same way, “and the earth shone with his glory”, and God says, “Here I will live among the Israelites forever.”

From under the threshold a stream begins to flow. It deepens from ankle-deep to a river too deep to cross, flows down to the Dead Sea and makes its salt water fresh: “Wherever the river goes, everything will live.” Trees grow on its banks, whose “leaves will never wither” and whose leaves are “for healing”. And the book ends with the name of the city.

Here too readers differ. Some expect a literal temple still to be built; many read the vision as a picture of the restored worship of God, fulfilled in Christ, who called his body the temple, and in the new Jerusalem of Revelation, where there is no temple, for “its temple is the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb”, and the river of the water of life flows with the tree of life on its banks.

How to read Ezekiel

Ezekiel is long and often strange, but it is well ordered, and the dates are a help: watch for them. Read the call (1–3), the departure of the glory (8–11), the turning point (33), the shepherds, the new heart and the dry bones (34–37), and the return of the glory and the river (43 and 47) first; they are the spine of the book.

Do not be put off by the visions. Ezekiel himself can barely describe them, and the details matter less than what they show: a God whose holiness cannot be domesticated, and who will not let his people go. Take the hard chapters slowly and in context; they are meant to shock. And listen for the refrain, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” It tells you what the whole book is for.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Ezekiel are worth knowing before you begin.

“The Lord GOD.” Ezekiel’s favourite way of naming God joins the word for “Lord” to God’s personal name. Where the name stands alone, this translation writes “the LORD”; where the two come together, it writes “the Lord GOD”, as in “Lord GOD, only you know.”

“Son of man.” God’s constant name for the prophet is kept as “Son of man”, so that readers can hear the phrase that Daniel and Jesus would later fill with new meaning; here it marks Ezekiel as a mortal before the glory of God.

The Spirit and the breath. The Hebrew ruach is translated by context: “the Spirit” who lifts the prophet, “breath” that enters the bones, the “four winds” from which it comes. In chapter 37 all three meet.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Ezekiel 1
fields.body_html:
Ezekiel’s vision by the Kebar Canal

1In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day, when I was living with the exiles beside the Kebar Canal, the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God. 2on the fifth day of the month (this was the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s exile), 3the word of the LORD came to the priest Ezekiel son of Buzi, there in the land of the Chaldeans beside the Kebar Canal. There the hand of the LORD came on him. 4As I looked, I saw a storm wind coming from the north: a huge cloud with fire flashing through it and brightness all around it. In the middle of the fire was something that looked like gleaming metal. 5Out of the middle of it came something that looked like four living creatures. This is what they looked like: they had the form of a human being. 6Each of them had four faces and four wings. 7Their legs were straight, and their feet were like a calf’s hooves. They sparkled like polished bronze. 8Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. As for the faces and wings of the four of them, 9their wings touched one another. As they moved they did not turn; each of them went straight ahead. 10This is what their faces looked like: each of the four had a human face, the face of a lion on the right, the face of an ox on the left, and the face of an eagle. 11Such were their faces. Their wings were spread out above them. Each had two wings that touched the wings of the creature on either side, and two that covered its body. 12Each one went straight ahead. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, and they did not turn as they moved. 13As for the appearance of the living creatures, they looked like burning coals of fire or like torches. Fire moved back and forth among the creatures. It was bright, and lightning flashed out of it. 14The living creatures darted back and forth like flashes of lightning. 15As I watched the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the ground next to each of the four creatures. 16The wheels and the way they were made looked like the sparkle of chrysolite. All four looked alike, and they seemed to be made like a wheel within a wheel. 17When they moved, they could go in any of the four directions without turning as they went. 18Their rims were high and awe-inspiring, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around. 19Whenever the living creatures moved, the wheels went along beside them, and whenever the creatures rose off the ground, the wheels rose as well. 20Wherever the spirit would go, they went, and the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. 21When the creatures went, the wheels went; when the creatures halted, the wheels halted; and when the creatures rose from the ground, the wheels rose with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. 22Over the heads of the living creatures was something like a vault, glittering like ice and awe-inspiring to see, spread out above their heads. 23Under the vault their wings were stretched out straight, one toward another, and each creature also had two wings covering its body. 24When they moved, I heard the sound of their wings. It was like the roar of rushing waters, like the voice of the Almighty, like the noise of an army camp. When they stood still, they lowered their wings. 25Then a voice came from above the vault over their heads, as they stood still with their wings lowered. 26Above the vault over their heads was something that looked like a throne, like sapphire in appearance. And on what looked like a throne, high above, was a figure that looked like a human being. 27From what looked like his waist upward, I saw something like gleaming metal, like fire enclosed all around. From what looked like his waist downward, I saw what looked like fire, and brightness surrounded him. 28Like a rainbow in the clouds on a day of rain, so was the brightness on every side. This was what the likeness of the glory of the LORD looked like. When I saw it, I fell face down, and I heard the voice of someone speaking.
fields.summary: Among the exiles by the Kebar Canal, Ezekiel sees a storm and four living creatures with wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with the likeness of the glory of God.

fields.title: Ezekiel 2
fields.body_html:
The LORD sends Ezekiel

1He said to me, “Son of man, stand up on your feet, and I will speak with you.” 2As he spoke to me, the Spirit came into me and stood me up on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me.

3He said to me, “Son of man, I am sending you to the Israelites, to rebellious nations that have revolted against me. They and their ancestors have rebelled against me to this very day. 4Their descendants are brazen and stubborn. I am sending you to them, and you will say to them, The Lord GOD says this. 5Whether they listen or refuse—for they are a rebellious house—they will come to know that a prophet has been among them.

6As for you, son of man, do not fear them or what they say, though thorns and briers surround you and you live among scorpions. Do not fear their words or be dismayed by their looks, for they are a rebellious house. 7You must speak my words to them, whether they listen or refuse, for they are rebellious.

A scroll to eat

8But you, son of man, listen to what I am saying to you. Do not rebel as that rebellious house does. Open your mouth and eat what I am giving you.” 9Then I looked, and I saw a hand stretched out toward me, and in it was a written scroll. 10He unrolled it in front of me, and it had writing on the front and on the back. Written on it were laments and mourning and woe.
fields.summary: God sends Ezekiel to the rebellious people of Israel, whether they listen or not, and gives him a scroll of lament and woe to eat.

fields.title: Ezekiel 3
fields.body_html:
Ezekiel eats the scroll

1He said to me, “Son of man, eat what is in front of you. Eat this scroll, and then go and speak to the house of Israel.” 2So I opened my mouth, and he gave me the scroll to eat. 3He said to me, “Son of man, eat this scroll I am giving you and fill your stomach with it.” So I ate it, and in my mouth it tasted as sweet as honey.

4He said to me, “Son of man, set out now for the house of Israel and speak my words to them. 5You are not being sent to a people of obscure speech and difficult language, but to the house of Israel, 6not to many peoples of obscure speech and difficult language, whose words you cannot understand. Surely, had I sent you to them, they would have listened to you. 7But the house of Israel will refuse to listen to you, because they refuse to listen to me. The whole house of Israel is hard-headed and stubborn. 8But I have made your face as hard as theirs, and your forehead as firm as their foreheads. 9I have made your forehead like diamond, harder than flint. Do not be afraid of them or terrified by their looks, for they are a rebellious house.”

Sent to the exiles

10He said to me, “Son of man, take to heart all my words that I speak to you, and listen closely. 11Go now to the exiles, to your own people, and speak to them. Say to them, The Lord GOD says this, whether they listen or refuse.” 12Then the Spirit lifted me up, and behind me I heard a great rumbling sound: “Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!” 13It was the sound of the living creatures’ wings brushing against one another, and of the wheels beside them: a great rumbling sound. 14The Spirit lifted me up and carried me off, and I went in bitterness and in the heat of my spirit, with the hand of the LORD pressing hard on me. 15I came to the exiles at Tel-abib, who lived by the Kebar Canal. I sat where they were living, and for seven days I sat among them, stunned. 16After the seven days were over, the word of the LORD came to me: 17Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel. When you hear a word from my mouth, you must warn them for me. 18If I say to a wicked person, “You will surely die,” and you do not warn them or speak out to turn them from their wicked way and save their life, that wicked person will die for their sin, but I will hold you responsible for their death. 19But if you warn the wicked and they do not turn from their wickedness or their wicked way, they will die for their sin, but you will have saved yourself.

20Again, if a righteous person turns away from their righteousness and does wrong, and I lay a stumbling block before them, they will die. Since you did not warn them, they will die for their sin, and the righteous things they did will not be remembered. But I will hold you responsible for their death. 21But if you warn the righteous person not to sin, and they do not sin, they will certainly live, because they took the warning, and you will have saved yourself.

Shut in and silenced

22There the hand of the LORD came on me, and he said to me, “Get up and go out into the valley, and there I will speak with you.” 23So I got up and went out into the valley, and there stood the glory of the LORD, like the glory I had seen by the Kebar Canal, and I fell face down. 24Then the Spirit came into me and set me on my feet, and he spoke with me and said, “Go and shut yourself inside your house. 25As for you, son of man, ropes will be put on you, and you will be tied up with them, so that you cannot go out among the people. 26I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you will be silent and unable to rebuke them, for they are a rebellious house. 27Whenever I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you will say to them, The Lord GOD says this. Whoever will listen, let them listen, and whoever refuses, let them refuse, for they are a rebellious house.”
fields.summary: The scroll tastes as sweet as honey. God makes Ezekiel a watchman for Israel and tells him he will be silent except when God gives him words.

fields.title: Ezekiel 4
fields.body_html:
The sign of the siege

1“Now, son of man, take a clay brick, set it in front of you, and draw on it a city, Jerusalem. 2Lay siege to it: build a siege wall against it, heap up a ramp against it, set up army camps around it, and place battering rams against it on every side. 3Then take an iron griddle and set it up as an iron wall between you and the city. Turn to face it. It will be under siege, and you will besiege it. This is a sign for the house of Israel.

Ezekiel lies on his side

4Then lie on your left side and lay the guilt of the house of Israel on it. For the number of days that you lie on that side, you will bear their guilt. 5I have assigned you a number of days equal to the years of their guilt, 390 days. So you will bear the guilt of the house of Israel. 6When you have completed these days, lie down again, this time on your right side, and bear the guilt of the house of Judah for forty days. I have assigned you one day for each year. 7Turn to face the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against the city. 8I will tie you up with ropes so that you cannot turn from one side to the other until you have finished the days of your siege. 9Take wheat and barley, beans and lentils, millet and spelt. Put them in one container and make bread for yourself from them. You are to eat it during the 390 days that you lie on your side. 10The food you eat is to be weighed out, about 8 ounces a day, and you are to eat it at set times. 11You are also to drink water by measure, about 2/3 quart, and drink it at set times. 12Eat it as you would a barley cake, baking it in their sight over dried human dung.”

13The LORD then said, “This is how the Israelites will eat their food, unclean, among the nations where I will drive them.” 14Then I said, “Oh, Lord GOD! I have never made myself unclean. From my youth until now I have never eaten anything that died by itself or was torn by wild animals, and no spoiled sacrificial meat has ever entered my mouth.”

15He said to me, “Very well, I will let you use cow dung instead of human dung. You may bake your bread over that.”

16He also said to me, “Son of man, I am about to break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. They will eat bread weighed out with anxiety and drink water measured out in despair, 17so that they will run short of bread and water. They will look at one another in horror and waste away under their guilt.”
fields.summary: Ezekiel acts out the siege of Jerusalem with a brick and lies on his side for many days, eating rationed food as a sign.

fields.title: Ezekiel 5
fields.body_html:
The sign of the shaved hair

1“As for you, son of man, take a sharp sword and use it as a barber’s razor. Shave your head and your beard with it. Then take scales for weighing and divide the hair into portions. 2When the days of the siege are over, burn a third of the hair in the fire inside the city. Take another third and strike it with the sword all around the city. Scatter the last third to the wind, and I will unsheathe a sword to pursue them. 3Take a few strands from these and tuck them into the fold of your robe. 4Take some of these again, throw them into the fire and burn them up. From it fire will spread to all the house of Israel.

This is Jerusalem

5The Lord GOD says this: This is Jerusalem. I have set her at the center of the nations, with countries all around her. 6But she has rebelled against my rulings more wickedly than the nations, and against my statutes more than the countries around her. Her people have rejected my rulings and have not lived by my statutes.

7Therefore the Lord GOD says this: You have been more unruly than the nations around you. You have not lived by my statutes or carried out my rulings. You have not even lived up to the standards of the nations around you.

8therefore the Lord GOD says this: I myself am against you, and I will carry out judgments among you in the sight of the nations. 9Because of all your detestable practices, I will do among you what I have never done before, and the like of which I will never do again.

10So parents among you will eat their children, and children will eat their parents. I will carry out judgments on you and scatter all your survivors to every wind.

11Therefore, as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, since you have made my sanctuary unclean with all your vile idols and all your detestable practices, I myself will cut you down. I will not look on you with pity or spare you. 12A third of your people will die of plague or perish from famine within your walls; a third will fall by the sword around you; and a third I will scatter to every wind and pursue with a drawn sword. 13Then my anger will be spent; I will satisfy my wrath on them and be appeased. Then they will know that I, the LORD, have spoken in my jealousy, when I spend my wrath on them. 14I will turn you into a ruin and an object of scorn among the nations around you, for every passerby to see. 15You will be a disgrace and an object of scorn, a warning and a horror for the nations around you, as I carry out judgments on you in anger and wrath and with furious rebukes. I, the LORD, have spoken. 16When I shoot at you the deadly arrows of famine, arrows meant for destruction that I send to destroy you, I will bring more and more famine on you and break your staff of bread. 17I will send famine and wild animals against you, and they will rob you of your children. Plague and bloodshed will pass through you, and I will bring the sword against you. I, the LORD, have spoken.”
fields.summary: Ezekiel shaves his head and divides the hair into thirds as a sign of what will happen to Jerusalem’s people.

fields.title: Ezekiel 6
fields.body_html:
Against the mountains of Israel

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, turn to face the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them. 3Say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! The Lord GOD says this to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: I myself am bringing a sword against you, and I will wipe out your high places. 4Your altars will be laid waste and your incense altars smashed, and I will make your slain fall in front of your idols. 5I will lay the corpses of the Israelites in front of their idols and scatter your bones around your altars. 6Wherever you live, the towns will be laid waste and the high places made desolate, so that your altars will be ruined and held guilty, your idols smashed and gone, your incense altars cut down, and what you have made wiped out. 7The slain will fall among you. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 8Yet I will spare some of you. Some will escape the sword and live among the nations when you are scattered through the countries. 9Then your survivors will remember me among the nations where they have been taken captive. They will remember how I was broken by their hearts, which prostituted themselves and turned away from me, and by their eyes, which prostituted themselves by going after their idols. They will loathe themselves for the evil they have done, for all their detestable practices. 10Then they will know that I am the LORD, and that I did not threaten in vain to bring this disaster on them.

Clap your hands and cry, Alas

11The Lord GOD says this: Clap your hands, stamp your foot and cry, “Alas!” over all the evil and detestable practices of the house of Israel, for they will fall by sword, famine and plague. 12Those far away will die of plague, those nearby will fall by the sword, and whoever is left and has been spared will die of famine. So I will spend my wrath on them. 13Then you will know that I am the LORD, as their slain are lying among their idols, around their altars, on every high hill and on all the mountaintops, under every spreading tree and every leafy oak, the places where they offered pleasing aromas to all their idols. 14I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land a desolate waste from the wilderness to Diblah, wherever they live. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
fields.summary: Ezekiel prophesies against the mountains of Israel, where idols are worshiped; the altars will be destroyed, but a remnant will remember God.

fields.title: Ezekiel 7
fields.body_html:
The end has come

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, the Lord GOD says this to the land of Israel: An end! The end has come to the four corners of the land. 3Now the end is upon you. I will unleash my anger against you, judge you by your ways, and bring all your detestable practices down on you. 4I will not look on you with pity or spare you. I will bring your ways down on you, and your detestable practices will remain among you. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

5The Lord GOD says this: Disaster! A disaster unlike any other! See, it is coming! 6An end has come! The end has come! It has woken up against you. See, it is coming! 7Doom has come to you who live in the land. The time has come, the day is close at hand: panic on the mountains, not shouts of joy. 8Very soon I will pour out my wrath on you and spend my anger against you. I will judge you by your ways and bring all your detestable practices down on you. 9I will not look on you with pity or spare you. I will bring your ways down on you, and your detestable practices will remain among you. Then you will know that I am the LORD, the one who strikes. 10See, the day! See, it is coming! Doom has gone out. The rod has blossomed; arrogance has sprouted. 11Violence has grown into a rod to punish wickedness. None of them will be left, none of their crowds, none of their wealth, and nothing of worth among them. 12The time has come; the day is here. The buyer should not rejoice, nor the seller grieve, for fierce anger is coming on all its crowds. 13Sellers will not get back what they sold, even if they are still alive, for the vision concerning all its crowds will not be revoked. Because of their sin, not one of them will hold on to life. 14They have sounded the trumpet and made everything ready, but no one goes out to fight, for my fierce anger is on all its crowds. 15The sword is outside, plague and famine inside. Whoever is in the countryside will die by the sword, and whoever is in the city will be devoured by famine and plague. 16Any who escape will flee to the mountains and be like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each over their own sin. 17Every hand will hang limp, and every knee will turn to water. 18They will put on sackcloth and be covered with terror. Shame will be on every face, and every head will be shaved. 19Their silver they will fling into the streets, and their gold will be something unclean. Their silver and their gold will not be able to save them on the day of the LORD’s fury. It cannot satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs, for it made them stumble into sin. 20They took pride in their beautiful jewelry and used it to make the images of their detestable practices and their vile idols. Therefore I will make it something unclean to them. 21I will hand it over as plunder to foreigners and as spoil to the wicked of the earth, and they will profane it. 22I will turn my face away from them, and they will profane my treasured place. Robbers will break into it and defile it.

Make a chain

23Make a chain! For the land is full of bloodshed, and the city is full of violence. 24I will bring the most evil of the nations to take over their houses. I will put an end to the pride of the powerful, and their holy places will be defiled. 25Terror is coming! They will look for peace, but there will be none. 26Disaster will follow disaster, and rumor will follow rumor. They will seek a vision from a prophet, but the priest will have no instruction to give, and the elders no counsel. 27The king will mourn, the prince will be clothed in despair, and the hands of the people of the land will shake with fear. I will deal with them according to their ways and judge them by the standards they themselves use. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
fields.summary: The end has come on the land, and God will judge Israel for its detestable practices.

fields.title: Ezekiel 8
fields.body_html:
The image of jealousy

1On the fifth day of the sixth month, in the sixth year, as I sat in my house with the elders of Judah seated before me, the hand of the Lord GOD fell on me there. 2I looked, and I saw something that looked like fire. From what appeared to be his waist down there was fire, and from his waist up there was something like a radiance, shining like gleaming metal. 3He reached out something that looked like a hand and took hold of me by a lock of my hair. The Spirit lifted me up between earth and sky and, in visions from God, brought me to Jerusalem, to the doorway of the inner court’s north gate, where the image of jealousy stood, the image that provokes jealousy. 4And there was the glory of the God of Israel, just as I had seen it in the vision in the plain. 5He said to me, “Son of man, look toward the north.” So I looked toward the north, and there, north of the altar gate, in the entrance itself, was this image of jealousy. 6He said to me, “Son of man, do you see the things they are doing, the terrible detestable practices that the house of Israel is committing here, which will drive me far from my sanctuary? But you will see even greater detestable practices.”

The elders in the dark

7Then he brought me to the entrance of the court, and when I looked, I saw a hole in the wall. 8He said to me, “Son of man, dig through the wall.” So I dug through the wall, and there was a doorway. 9He said to me, “Go in and see the wicked detestable practices they are committing here.” 10So I went in and looked, and there, carved all around on the wall, were all kinds of creeping things and beasts, detestable things, and all the idols of the house of Israel. 11In front of them stood seventy of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan stood in the middle of them. Every man held his censer, and a fragrant cloud of incense rose up. 12He said to me, “Son of man, do you see what the elders of the house of Israel practice in darkness, each in the room of his own carved image? They say, ‘The LORD does not see us; the LORD has abandoned the land.’” 13He said to me, “You will see them committing even greater detestable practices.” 14Next he brought me to the doorway of the north gate of the house of the LORD. Women were sitting there, weeping for Tammuz.

Bowing to the sun

15He said to me, “Do you see this, son of man? You will see even greater detestable practices than these.” 16Then he brought me into the inner court of the house of the LORD. There, at the doorway of the LORD’s temple, between the porch and the altar, stood about twenty-five men. They had turned their backs on the temple of the LORD and were facing east, bowing down to the sun in the east. 17He said to me, “Do you see this, son of man? Is it not enough that the house of Judah commits the detestable practices it has committed here? Must they also fill the land with violence and provoke me to anger again and again? Look, they are putting the branch to their nose! 18So I too will act in wrath. I will not look on them with pity or spare them. Though they cry out in my ears with a loud voice, I will not listen to them.”
fields.summary: In a vision Ezekiel is taken to Jerusalem and sees idolatry in the temple: elders burning incense to images, women weeping for Tammuz and men worshiping the sun.

fields.title: Ezekiel 9
fields.body_html:
Six men with weapons

1Then he cried out in my hearing with a loud voice, “Come near, you who are appointed to punish the city, each with his weapon of destruction in his hand!” 2Then six men came from the direction of the upper gate that faces north, each with a weapon for smashing in his hand. Among them was a man dressed in linen, with a scribe’s writing case at his side. They came in and took their places beside the bronze altar. 3Now the glory of the God of Israel had risen from above the cherub where it had rested, and had moved to the threshold of the temple. He called to the man dressed in linen who had the writing case at his side.

A mark on the foreheads

4The LORD said to him, “Go all through the city, all through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the people who sigh and groan over all the detestable practices committed in it.” 5To the others he said in my hearing, “Follow him through the city and strike. Do not look on them with pity or spare them. 6Kill old men, young men and young women, little children and women, until none are left; but do not go near anyone who has the mark. Start at my sanctuary.” So they began with the elders standing in front of the temple. 7He said to them, “Defile the temple and fill its courts with the dead. Go!” So they went out and struck people down throughout the city. 8While they were striking them down and I was left alone, I fell on my face and cried out, “Oh, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all who remain of Israel as you pour out your wrath on Jerusalem?” 9He said to me, “The guilt of the house of Israel and Judah is immense. The land is full of bloodshed and the city full of injustice. For they say, ‘The LORD has abandoned the land; the LORD does not see.’” 10As for me, I will not look on them with pity or spare them; I will bring their conduct down on their own heads.” 11Then the man dressed in linen, with the writing case at his side, came back with a report: “I have done as you commanded me.”
fields.summary: Six executioners strike down the city’s idolaters, but first a man in linen marks those who grieve over the city’s sins.

fields.title: Ezekiel 10
fields.body_html:
The cherubim and the glory

1I looked, and on the vault above the heads of the cherubim I saw something that looked like a sapphire stone, something that looked like a throne, appearing above them. 2He said to the man dressed in linen, “Go in among the whirling wheels beneath the cherub. Take two handfuls of burning coals from among the cherubim and toss them over the city.” He went in while I watched. 3The cherubim were standing on the south side of the temple when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court. 4Then the glory of the LORD rose from above the cherub and moved to the threshold of the temple. Cloud filled the temple, and the court was flooded with the radiance of the glory of the LORD. 5The sound of the cherubim’s wings carried to the outer court. It was like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks. 6When he had given the man dressed in linen the command, “Take fire from among the whirling wheels, from among the cherubim,” the man went in and stood beside one of the wheels. 7Then one of the cherubim reached out its hand from among the cherubim to the fire that was among them. It took some and put it into the hands of the man dressed in linen, who took it and went out. 8Under their wings the cherubim could be seen to have something that looked like human hands. 9I looked, and there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one wheel beside each cherub. The wheels gleamed like chrysolite. 10As for their appearance, all four had the same form, as if a wheel were inside a wheel. 11When they moved, they could go in any of the four directions without turning as they went. Wherever the head faced, the wheels followed it, without turning as they went. 12Their whole bodies, their backs, their hands and their wings, and the wheels too, were full of eyes all around, the wheels that the four of them had. 13As for the wheels, I heard them called “the whirling wheels.” 14Each one had four faces: the first was the face of a cherub, the second a human face, the third a lion’s face and the fourth an eagle’s face. 15Then the cherubim rose up. These were the living creatures I had seen by the Kebar Canal. 16When the cherubim moved, the wheels moved beside them, and when the cherubim spread their wings to rise from the ground, the wheels stayed at their side. 17When the cherubim stood still, the wheels stood still, and when they rose, the wheels rose with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them. 18Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the temple and stopped above the cherubim. 19As I watched, the cherubim spread their wings and rose from the ground, and they went out with the wheels beside them. They halted at the entrance to the east gate of the LORD’s house, with the glory of the God of Israel above them. 20These were the living creatures I saw under the God of Israel at the Kebar Canal, and I knew that they were cherubim. 21Each had four faces and four wings, and under their wings was something that looked like human hands. 22As for their faces, they were the very faces I had seen by the Kebar Canal, in how they looked and in what they were. Each one went straight ahead.
fields.summary: The glory of God rises from the cherubim and moves to the threshold of the temple.

fields.title: Ezekiel 11
fields.body_html:
Twenty-five men at the east gate

1Then the Spirit lifted me up and carried me to the east gate of the house of the LORD, the gate facing east. At its entrance were twenty-five men, and I saw among them Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, officials of the people.

2He said to me, “Son of man, these men are the ones plotting evil and giving wicked advice in this city, 3who say, ‘The time for building houses is not near. This city is the pot, and we are the meat.’ 4So prophesy against them; prophesy, son of man!” 5Then the Spirit of the LORD fell on me, and he said to me, “Say: The LORD says this: That is what you are saying, house of Israel, but I know the thoughts that rise in your minds. 6You have killed many people in this city and filled its streets with the dead.

7Therefore the Lord GOD says this: The dead you have laid in the city are the meat, and this city is the pot; but you I will take out of it. 8You fear the sword, and the sword is what I will bring against you, declares the Lord GOD. 9I will take you out of the city and hand you over to foreigners, and I will carry out judgments against you. 10You will fall by the sword; I will judge you at the border of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 11This city will not be your pot, and you will not be the meat inside it. I will judge you at the border of Israel. 12Then you will know that I am the LORD. You have not followed my statutes or carried out my rulings; instead you have acted by the rulings of the nations around you.” 13While I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died. Then I fell face down and cried out with a loud voice, “Oh, Lord GOD! Are you going to wipe out the remnant of Israel completely?”

A sanctuary for the exiles

14The word of the LORD came to me: 15Son of man, your brothers, your own brothers, the relatives who have the right to redeem you, and the whole house of Israel, all of them, are the ones of whom the people of Jerusalem have said, “Stay far away from the LORD! It is to us that this land has been given as a possession.”

16Therefore say: The Lord GOD says this: Though I have sent them far off among the nations and scattered them through the lands, for a little while I have still been a sanctuary to them in the lands they have gone to.

17Therefore say: The Lord GOD says this: I will gather you from the peoples and bring you together from the lands where you have been scattered, and I will give the land of Israel to you. 18When they come there, they will remove from it all its vile idols and all its detestable practices. 19I will give them one heart and put a new spirit within them. I will take the heart of stone out of their bodies and give them a heart of flesh, 20so that they will follow my statutes and carefully carry out my rulings. They will be my people, and I will be their God. 21But as for those whose hearts are devoted to their vile idols and detestable practices, I will bring their conduct down on their own heads, declares the Lord GOD. 22Then the cherubim spread their wings, with the wheels beside them, while the glory of the God of Israel was above them. 23The glory of the LORD went up from the middle of the city and stopped over the mountain east of the city. 24Then the Spirit lifted me up and, in the vision given by the Spirit of God, brought me back to the exiles in Chaldea. And the vision I had seen left me. 25And I told the exiles everything that the LORD had shown me.
fields.summary: God judges Jerusalem’s leaders and promises to give the exiles a new heart and a new spirit. The glory of God leaves the city.

fields.title: Ezekiel 12
fields.body_html:
Baggage for exile

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, you live among a rebellious house. They have eyes that can see, yet they do not see, and ears that can hear, yet they do not hear, because they are a rebellious house. 3So you, son of man, pack your belongings for exile, and in daylight, while they watch, set out as one going into exile. Go from your place to another place while they watch. Perhaps they will understand, rebellious house though they are. 4Bring out your belongings by day while they watch, like belongings packed for exile. Then in the evening, while they watch, go out yourself like people going into exile. 5As they look on, dig a hole in the wall and take your belongings out through it. 6While they watch, lift the bundle onto your shoulder and carry it out in the dark. Cover your face so that you do not see the land, for I have made you a sign for the house of Israel. 7So I did as I was commanded. By day I brought out my belongings as if packed for exile, and in the evening I dug through the wall with my hands. I took them out in the dark, carrying them on my shoulder while they watched.

8In the morning the word of the LORD came to me: 9Son of man, has not the house of Israel, that rebellious house, asked you, “What are you doing?” 10Say to them: The Lord GOD says this: This oracle is about the prince in Jerusalem and the whole house of Israel living there. 11Say: I am a sign for you. As I have done, so it will be done to them. They will go into exile, into captivity. 12The prince among them will lift his bundle onto his shoulder in the dark and go out. They will dig through the wall to get him out through it. He will cover his face so that he cannot see the land with his eyes. 13I will spread my net over him, and he will be trapped in my snare. I will take him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, but he will not see it, and he will die there. 14All those around him, his helpers and all his troops, I will scatter to every wind, and I will draw the sword to pursue them. 15Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I scatter them among the nations and spread them across the lands. 16But I will spare a few of them from the sword, famine and plague, so that among the nations where they go they may tell about all their detestable practices. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

Bread eaten with trembling

17The word of the LORD came to me: 18Son of man, eat your food trembling, and drink your water shaking with anxiety. 19Say to the people of the land: The Lord GOD says this about those who live in Jerusalem, in the land of Israel: They will eat their food with anxiety and drink their water in horror, for their land will be stripped of all it holds because of the violence of everyone who lives there. 20The cities where people live will be laid waste, and the land will become a desolation. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

Every vision will come true

21The word of the LORD came to me: 22Son of man, what is this proverb you have about the land of Israel: “The days go on and on, and every vision comes to nothing”? 23Therefore say to them: The Lord GOD says this: I will put an end to this proverb, and they will not quote it in Israel anymore. Tell them instead: The days are near when every vision will be fulfilled. 24For there will be no more false visions or flattering divination among the house of Israel. 25For I am the LORD. I will speak whatever word I speak, and it will be done without further delay. In your own days, you rebellious house, I will speak the word and carry it out, declares the Lord GOD.

26The word of the LORD came to me: 27Son of man, the house of Israel is saying, “The vision he sees is for many days to come; he prophesies about times far away.” 28Therefore say to them: The Lord GOD says this: None of my words will be put off any longer. Whatever I say will be done, declares the Lord GOD.
fields.summary: Ezekiel packs his bags and digs through the wall as a sign of exile.

fields.title: Ezekiel 13
fields.body_html:
Against the false prophets

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who are prophesying now. Say to those who prophesy out of their own minds: Hear the word of the LORD! 3The Lord GOD says this: Woe to the senseless prophets who go after their own spirit and have seen nothing! 4Your prophets, Israel, have been like jackals among ruins. 5You have not gone up into the breaches or rebuilt the wall for the house of Israel, so that it might stand firm in battle on the day of the LORD. 6Their visions are false and their divination is a lie. They say, “The LORD declares,” though the LORD has not sent them, and yet they expect their word to come true. 7Is it not a false vision you have seen, and a lying divination you have spoken, when you say, “The LORD declares,” though I myself have not spoken?

The whitewashed wall

8Therefore the Lord GOD says this: Because you have spoken empty words and seen lying visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD. 9My hand will turn against the prophets whose visions are false and whose divinations are lies. They will have no place in the council of my people, they will not be recorded in the register of the house of Israel, and they will not set foot on Israel’s soil. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD. 10This is because they have misled my people by saying, “Peace,” when there is no peace. When someone builds a flimsy wall, they cover it with whitewash. 11Tell those who cover it with whitewash that it will fall. Torrents of rain will come; you hailstones will fall, and a violent wind will burst out. 12When the wall falls, will people not ask you, “Where is the whitewash you covered it with?”

13Therefore the Lord GOD says this: In my wrath I will let loose a violent wind; in my anger there will be torrents of rain, and hailstones in fury to destroy it. 14I will tear down the wall you covered with whitewash and level it to the ground, so that its foundation is laid bare. When it falls, you will be destroyed under it. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 15I will spend my wrath on the wall and on those who covered it with whitewash, and I will say to you, “Gone is the wall, and gone are those who whitewashed it,” 16those prophets of Israel who prophesied to Jerusalem and saw visions of peace for her, though there was no peace, declares the Lord GOD.

Against women who prophesy falsely

17Now you, son of man, turn to face the women of your people who prophesy out of their own minds, and prophesy against them, 18and say: The Lord GOD says this: Woe to the women who sew bands for everyone’s wrists and make head veils for people of every height, to hunt down lives! Will you hunt down the lives of my people and keep yourselves alive? 19For a few handfuls of barley and scraps of bread you have profaned me among my people. You have put to death people who should not die and kept alive people who should not live, by lying to my people, who listen to lies.

20Therefore the Lord GOD says this: I am against your bands, with which you hunt down lives as if they were birds. I will tear them from your arms and set free the lives you hunt down like birds. 21I will tear off your veils and rescue my people from your power, and they will no longer be caught in your grip. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 22Because with your lies you have discouraged the righteous, whom I had not made to grieve, and you have strengthened the hands of the wicked, so that they do not turn from their evil ways and save their lives, 23So you will see no more false visions and practice no more divination. I will rescue my people from your power. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
fields.summary: Ezekiel condemns the false prophets who say “Peace” when there is no peace, like those who whitewash a flimsy wall.

fields.title: Ezekiel 14
fields.body_html:
Idols in the heart

1Some of the elders of Israel came to me and sat down in front of me.

2The word of the LORD came to me: 3Son of man, these men have taken idols into their hearts and placed before their faces the stumbling block that leads them into guilt. Should I let them consult me at all?

4Therefore speak to them and tell them: The Lord GOD says this: When anyone of the house of Israel sets up idols in their heart, puts the stumbling block of their guilt before their face, and then goes to the prophet, I the LORD myself will give that person an answer, as the great number of their idols deserves, 5so that I may lay hold of the hearts of the house of Israel, who have all turned away from me to their idols.

6Therefore say to the house of Israel: The Lord GOD says this: Repent! Turn away from your idols, and turn your faces away from all your detestable practices. 7For if anyone of the house of Israel, or of the outsiders who live in Israel, separates themselves from me, sets up idols in their heart, puts the stumbling block of their guilt before their face, and then comes to a prophet to inquire of me through him, I the LORD will answer that person myself. 8I will set my face against that person and make them a sign and a byword. I will cut them off from my people. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

9And if the prophet is deceived and speaks a message, it is I, the LORD, who have deceived that prophet. I will raise my hand against him and wipe him out from among my people Israel. 10Both will bear their guilt; the guilt of the prophet will be the same as the guilt of the one who consulted him, 11so that the house of Israel will no longer stray from me or defile themselves with all their rebellions. They will be my own people, and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD.

Noah, Daniel and Job

12The word of the LORD came to me: 13Son of man, suppose a land sins against me by being unfaithful, and I stretch out my hand against it, break its supply of bread, send famine on it and cut off from it both people and animals, 14even if these three men, Noah, Daniel and Job, were living there, their righteousness would save only themselves, declares the Lord GOD. 15Or if I sent wild animals through the land and they left it childless, so that it became a desolation that no one would pass through because of the animals, 16even if these three men were in it, as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, they could not rescue sons or daughters. They alone would be rescued, and the land would become a desolation. 17Or if I brought a sword against that land and said, “Let the sword pass through the land,” and cut off from it both people and animals, 18even if these three men were in it, as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, they could not rescue sons or daughters; they alone would be rescued. 19Or if I sent plague into that land and poured out my wrath on it in bloodshed, to cut off from it both people and animals, 20even if Noah, Daniel and Job were in it, as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, they could save neither son nor daughter. They would save only themselves by their righteousness.

21For the Lord GOD says this: How much worse it will be when I send my four terrible judgments against Jerusalem, sword, famine, wild animals and plague, to cut off from it both people and animals! 22Yet there will be survivors left in it, sons and daughters brought out of it. When they come out to you and you see their conduct and their actions, you will be consoled over the disaster I have brought on Jerusalem, over everything I have brought on it. 23They will console you when you see their conduct and their actions, for you will know that I did not act without reason in all that I did there, declares the Lord GOD.
fields.summary: God will not answer idolaters who come to inquire. Even Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves.

fields.title: Ezekiel 15
fields.body_html:
The wood of the vine

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, how is the wood of the vine any better than other wood, than a branch among the trees of the forest? 3Can wood be taken from it to make anything useful? Can anyone make a peg from it to hang things on? 4No, it is thrown into the fire as fuel. When the fire has burned up both ends and the middle is charred, is it good for anything? 5Even when it was whole, it could not be made into anything useful. How much less can it be made into anything useful once the fire has burned it and it is charred!

6Therefore the Lord GOD says this: As with the vine’s wood among the forest trees, which I have handed over to the fire to burn, so I will hand over the people who live in Jerusalem. 7I will set my face against them. They have come out of the fire, but the fire will still burn them up. Then you will know that I am the LORD, when I turn my face against them. 8I will make the land a desolation because they have been unfaithful, declares the Lord GOD.
fields.summary: Jerusalem is like a useless vine, fit only for burning.

fields.title: Ezekiel 16
fields.body_html:
Jerusalem, the abandoned child and the unfaithful wife

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, confront Jerusalem with her detestable practices, 3and say, The Lord GOD says this to Jerusalem: You came from the land of the Canaanites; that is where you were born. Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. 4On the day you were born, no one cut your umbilical cord or washed you with water to clean you. No one rubbed you with salt or wrapped you in cloths. 5No one looked on you with pity or cared enough to do any of these things for you. Instead, you were thrown out on the open ground, because your life was despised on the day you were born. 6Then I passed by you and saw you thrashing about in your blood. There in your blood I said to you, “Live!” There in your blood I said to you, “Live!” 7I made you flourish like a plant in the field. You grew up, became tall and reached the age of full beauty. Your breasts were formed and your hair had grown, but you were still naked and bare. 8Then I passed by you again and saw you, and you were old enough for love. So I spread the corner of my cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I gave you my solemn oath and entered into a covenant with you, declares the Lord GOD, and you became mine. 9Then I bathed you with water, washed the blood off you and anointed you with oil. 10I dressed you in embroidered clothing and put sandals of fine leather on your feet. I wrapped you in fine linen and covered you with costly fabric. 11I adorned you with jewelry. I put bracelets on your arms and a necklace around your neck. 12I put a ring in your nose, earrings in your ears and a beautiful crown on your head. 13So you were adorned with gold and silver, and your clothes were of fine linen, costly fabric and embroidered cloth. You ate the finest flour, honey and olive oil. You became very beautiful indeed, and you rose to be a queen. 14Your fame spread among the nations because of your beauty. It was perfect because of my splendor that I had put on you, declares the Lord GOD. 15But you trusted in your beauty and used your fame to prostitute yourself. You poured out your prostitution on everyone who passed by, and anyone could have you. 16You took some of your clothes and made colorful shrines for yourself on the high places, and there you prostituted yourself. Nothing like this has ever happened, and it never should. 17You took your fine jewelry, made of my gold and silver that I had given you, and made yourself male images, and you prostituted yourself with them. 18You took your embroidered clothes and dressed them, and you set my oil and my incense before them. 19The food I gave you, the fine flour, oil and honey I fed you with, you set before them as an offering with a pleasing aroma. That is what happened, declares the Lord GOD. 20You took your sons and daughters, whom you had borne to me, and sacrificed them to the idols as food. Was your prostitution not enough, 21that you slaughtered my children and gave them up to the idols, making them pass through the fire? 22In all your detestable practices and your prostitution, you never once remembered your early days, when you were naked and bare, thrashing about in your blood. 23After all your wickedness (woe, woe to you! declares the Lord GOD), 24you built yourself a platform and made yourself a lofty shrine in every public square. 25At the head of every street you built your lofty shrine and made your beauty something detestable. You spread your legs for everyone who passed by and multiplied your prostitution. 26You prostituted yourself with the Egyptians, your lustful neighbors, and you multiplied your prostitution to provoke me to anger. 27So I stretched out my hand against you and cut down your allotted portion. I handed you over to the will of those who hate you, the Philistine cities, who were shocked by your lewd behavior. 28You prostituted yourself with the Assyrians too, because you could not be satisfied. You prostituted yourself with them, and even then you were not satisfied. 29You multiplied your prostitution with Chaldea, the land of traders, and even this did not satisfy you. 30How sick your heart is, declares the Lord GOD, that you do all these things, the deeds of a shameless prostitute, 31building your platform at the head of every street and making your lofty shrine in every public square! Yet you were not like a prostitute, because you scorned payment. 32You adulterous wife, who takes strangers instead of her husband! 33All prostitutes are given gifts, but you gave your gifts to all your lovers. You paid them bribes so that they would come from every side for your prostitution. 34So in your prostitution you were the opposite of other women. No one came after you to hire you; you paid, and no one paid you. You were the opposite. 35Therefore, you prostitute, hear the word of the LORD.

The sentence on the unfaithful wife

36The Lord GOD says this: Because you poured out your lust and exposed your nakedness as you prostituted yourself with your lovers and with all your detestable idols, and because you gave them the blood of your children, 37therefore I am about to gather all your lovers whom you pleased, everyone you loved and everyone you hated. I will bring them against you from all around and strip you naked in front of them, and they will see all your nakedness. 38I will sentence you as women who commit adultery and murder are sentenced, and I will bring on you the bloodshed of my wrath and jealousy. 39I will hand you over to them, and they will tear down your platform and demolish your lofty shrines. They will strip you of your clothes and take away your fine jewelry, leaving you naked and bare. 40They will bring up a mob against you, and they will stone you and cut you to pieces with their swords. 41They will burn down your houses and carry out judgments on you while many women look on. I will stop your prostitution, and you will never again pay your lovers. 42Then I will satisfy my wrath on you, and my jealousy will turn away from you. I will be calm and no longer angry. 43Since you forgot the days of your youth and provoked me with all these things, I in turn will bring your deeds down on your own head, declares the Lord GOD. Did you not add lewdness to all your other detestable practices? 44Everyone who quotes proverbs will quote this one about you: “Like mother, like daughter.” 45You are truly your mother’s daughter, who despised her husband and her children. And you are truly the sister of your sisters, who despised their husbands and their children. The mother of you all was a Hittite and your father an Amorite. 46Your older sister is Samaria, who lived with her daughters to the north of you, and your younger sister, who lived with her daughters to the south of you, is Sodom. 47You did not just walk in their ways and copy their detestable practices. As if that were not enough, you became more corrupt than they were in all your ways. 48As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, not even your sister Sodom and her daughters did what you and your daughters have done. 49This was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, more food than they needed and careless ease, but they did not help the poor and needy. 50They were haughty and did detestable things before me, so I removed them when I saw it.

More guilty than her sisters

51Samaria did not commit even half the sins you have. You have done far more detestable things than they did, and by all the detestable things you have done you have made your sisters look righteous. 52So you too must bear your disgrace, for you have argued the case for your sisters. Because your sins were more detestable than theirs, they are more righteous than you. So be ashamed, and bear your disgrace, for you have made your sisters look righteous. 53But I will restore their fortunes, the fortunes of Sodom and her daughters and the fortunes of Samaria and her daughters, and I will restore your fortunes along with theirs, 54so that you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you have done, and so become a comfort to them. 55As for your sisters, Sodom and her daughters and Samaria and her daughters will go back to what they were before, and you and your daughters will also go back to what you were before. 56Was not your sister Sodom a byword on your lips in the days of your pride, 57before your own wickedness was exposed? Now you are the object of scorn for the daughters of Aram and all her neighbors, and for the daughters of the Philistines, who despise you on every side. 58You must bear the penalty of your lewdness and your detestable practices, declares the LORD.

An everlasting covenant

59For the Lord GOD says this: I will deal with you as you deserve, because you despised the oath and broke the covenant. 60Yet I myself will remember the covenant I made with you in your youth, and I will establish with you a covenant that is everlasting. 61Then you will remember your ways and feel ashamed as you welcome your sisters, both older and younger. I will give them to you as daughters, though not on the basis of your covenant. 62I will establish my own covenant with you. Then you will know that I am the LORD, 63so that you will remember and feel ashamed, and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, when I make atonement for you for all you have done, declares the Lord GOD.
fields.summary: God tells the story of Jerusalem as an abandoned baby whom God raised and married, who became unfaithful. Yet God will remember the covenant and make an everlasting covenant with her.

fields.title: Ezekiel 17
fields.body_html:
The riddle of the two eagles

1The word of the LORD came to me: 2Son of man, pose a riddle and tell a parable to the house of Israel, 3and say, The Lord GOD says this: A great eagle with great wings and long feathers, full of plumage of many colors, came to Lebanon and took hold of the top of the cedar. 4It plucked off the topmost of its young shoots and carried it to a land of merchants, and it set it down in a city of traders. 5Then it took a seed from the land and planted it in a fertile field. It set it like a willow shoot beside abundant water. 6It sprouted and became a low, spreading vine. Its branches turned toward the eagle, and its roots stayed under it. So it became a vine, producing shoots and sending out branches. 7But there was another great eagle with great wings and thick plumage. And look, this vine bent its roots toward it and stretched out its branches to it from the beds where it was planted, so that it might water it. 8Yet it had been planted in good soil beside abundant water, where it could produce branches, bear fruit and become a splendid vine.

Will the vine thrive?

9Say, The Lord GOD says this: Will it thrive? Will the first eagle not tear up its roots and strip off its fruit, so that it withers? All its fresh new leaves will wither. He will need no strong arm or great army to pull it up by its roots. 10Look, it is planted, but will it thrive? Will it not wither completely when the east wind strikes it? It will wither in the beds where it sprouted.

The riddle explained

11The word of the LORD came to me: 12Ask the rebellious house, “Do you not know what these things mean?” Then tell them, The king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, took its king and its officials, and brought them back with him to Babylon. 13He took a member of the royal family, made a covenant with him and put him under oath.
